name: Mapos Buang
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Hooley, Bruce A. 1970. Mapos Buang - Territory of New Guinea. PhD dissertation, University of Pennsylvania (full grammar plausibly covering stress); SIL Mapos Buang dictionary (2022)

new_statements.quote: [ə] is a prominent feature of Buang phonology, being as it is the open transition between consonants both within words and between words. It could be regarded as neutralisation of the vowels in the unstressed position. It is always unstressed [...] The only other vowel which occurs in unstressed syllables is a. Since shewa only occurs in unstressed syllables, it is not usually confused by native speakers with the full vowel of stressed syllables even if that vowel is an e. [...] if e occurs more than once in a word, the stressed e is marked é as in ggévek 'crawl', ḳekén 'variety of edible grass'.
new_statements.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. & Mose Lung Rambok (comps.). 2010. Ḳapiya Tateḳin Buang Vuheng-atov Ayej = Central Buang–English Dictionary. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics, Papua New Guinea Branch. 672 pp.
new_statements.locator: Introduction, 'Orthographical decisions', point 3, p. 11 (PDF p. 15); cf. draft Hooley 2006, p. 6
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (676 pp., pdftk 2010 output, text layer present). extracted text of PDF p. 15 = printed p. 11, section 'Orthographical decisions', point 3, reads exactly: '[ə] is a prominent feature of Buang phonology, being as it is the open transition between consonants both within words and between words. It could be regarded as neutralisation of the vowels in the unstressed position. It is always unstressed and could be omitted from the orthography, nevertheless, to prevent the sometime appearance in text of long sequences of consonants, and possible confusion with digraphs, it has been written. It also gives text a more "normal" appearance. The symbol chosen was e, since in some songs the shewa i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional rule is stated in any accessible source. Hooley's explicit generalisations are (i) unstressed syllables contain only schwa or a, i.e. any full (non-a) vowel is stressed, and (ii) long vowels are always stressed (Hooley 1962a:10 as reported by Sankoff 1968:94). Position within the word is otherwise lexical: the 2010 dictionary marks stress on every headword and needs an é diacritic to disambiguate stressed e; verbs 'stressed on the first syllable' vs. not form a morphological class (a-/na-/se- allomorphy). Counting the dictionary's 3,871 stress-marked transcriptions: disyllables are 71% final-stressed (a.ˈmaⁿd) vs 29% initial (ˈa.ma); trisyllables 79% penult, 13% final, 9% initial — i.e. stress sits on the (last) full-vowel syllable of the root, with reduced/prefixal initial syllables unstressed, but pairs like aga [ˈa.ᵑɡa] 'cob' vs aġa [a.ˈᵑɢa] 'eat' show it is not predictable from segments alone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the 2010 dictionary transcriptions occasionally carry ˌ on an initial syllable (e.g. ˌa.ʁe.ˈᵐbu), without explanation.
new_statements.exceptions: Sankoff 1968:94-95 notes that in the headwater dialect (her Dialect A) the long-vowel rule is inapplicable (length not phonemic there) and that vowel shifts 'frequently change the stress from syllable to syllable' between dialects and villages; Hooley 2010 notes clitics ba=/be=, ga=/ge=, ma=/me= occur unstressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, dictionary citation forms (Mapos I village speech, Central Buang); the 'ner niweek' (ˈ) mark in the 2010 dictionary is a per-word lexical stress mark.
new_statements.identity_note: Central Buang = Mapos Buang [bzh], mapo1242. The dictionaries describe the speech of Mapos I village (the 'Mapos' dialect; Hooley 1976:341 distinguishes Mapos Buang from the headwater dialect within Central Buang). Sankoff 1968's Dialect B = Mapos/Central Buang, Dialect A = headwater dialect (also mapo1242), Dialect C = Mangga Buang (mang1404, a separate language). Adams & Lauck 1985's stress remarks concern the Mumeng dialect chain (Patep etc.), not this language.

sources.locator: Introduction, 'Orthographical decisions', point 3, p. 11 (PDF p. 15); cf. draft Hooley 2006, p. 6
sources.note: Intro 'Sound system & orthography' (pp. 9-12): no positional rule; states that schwa is 'neutralisation of the vowels in the unstressed position', 'always unstressed', that 'the only other vowel which occurs in unstressed syllables is a', and that where e occurs twice in a word 'the stressed e is marked é' (p. 11). Grammar intro distinguishes verbs 'stressed on the first syllable' as a morphological class (pp. 17-19; entries a-, na-, se-, n-). Every headword carries an IPA transcription with a stress mark (ˈ, key p. 4 'ner niweek'): my count over 3,871 marked forms gives 2-syll. words 1452 fi…

sources.citation: Adams, Karen & Linda Lauck. 1985. Dialect survey of Mumeng dialect chain. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 22 (PL A-63), 1-28.
sources.note: About the Mumeng chain (Patep etc.), not Central Buang: 'Initial unstressed syllables in Patep always have the vowel schwa... Kumalu, Mumengtein, and Pelenkwa have a different stress pattern, so that not only does the initial syllable have a full vowel, but it also receives stress' (p. 11). Mentions Mapos Buang only for comparison of verb morphology.

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. 1974. Orthography problems in Central Buang. Kivung 7(2): 82-90.
sources.note: Scan without text layer, scanned. Phoneme chart (p. 85) and: 'there is a non-phonemic transitional schwa occurring between words and in unstressed syllables unless the vowel is a' (p. 85); 'all vowels other than a are neutralized in the unstressed syllable' (p. 88). No statement of where stress falls.

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. (comp.). 2006. Mapos Buang dictionary (draft, work in progress). 407 pp. SIL archive entry 31034.
sources.note: pp. 3-6 sound system: 'There is an open transition between consonants which manifests itself as a shewa in unstressed syllables... since shewa only occurs in unstressed syllables, Buang speakers do not confuse it with the full e of stressed syllables' (p. 6); 'Verbs stressed on the first syllable of the root have a prefix a- in the first person plural inclusive' (p. 8). No placement rule; no stress marks on headwords in this draft.

sources.note: Ch. 5 phonology outline of Buang dialects A (headwater), B (Mapos/Central), C (Mangga). p. 94: 'Hooley's basic rule of stress (1962a:10), i.e. that long vowels are always stressed'; pp. 94-95: 'Although the stress rules as enunciated in Hooley (1962a) may differ little from Dialect A to B... shifts in vowel sounds in various words frequently change the stress from syllable to syllable'; p. 95: Hooley's 'rule that in unstressed syllables the only contrast is between /a/ and non-/a/'. Second-hand on Hooley 1962a; gives no positional rule.
